utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mazrekaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will now continue. Please remember that the declaration you gave at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth continues to apply to the evidence this morning. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mazrekaj. Yesterday we were --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- we were at the point where you said that you and the villagers decided to leave because you were forced out, and you went to Carrabreg, to the check-point of the Serbian police to ask them if you could pass through the check-point. That's correct? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well, but I have to make a clarification because this is the second time we left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the first time you left the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was when the first shelling happened, when Decani and other villages, surrounding villages, were shelled in May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. We are speaking now - and this is where we left off - about the 23rd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now refer to the fourth full paragraph of page 5 of the English, and this is the first paragraph of page 5 of the Serb version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in your statement, sir, at page 5, I believe you have it there, that the police at the check-point asked you about the number of villagers and you told them there was 520 and that they let you go back to the village and would be waiting for you there. Let me just read the thing: "They let me go back to the village and would be waiting for us there." I take it from that that the police at the check-point told you could pass through the check-point with the villagers. Is that correct? Can you answer orally, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues and me were stopped there and I told them, Can we pass through this check-point? They asked me, How many villagers do you have? And I said, I have 520 and we need to go to Isniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I want to found out is you said that when you returned to Drenoc --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's the next paragraph, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- you told the villagers not to go through Carrabreg because they would separate the men from the women and children. Why did you tell the villagers not to go through that check-point?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We told the villagers that because those things were happening every day. Women were separated from the men, and that's why I said that to the villagers, because I feared the same would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: According to your statement, eventually yourself and the villagers left and went to Beleg?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were at Beleg, did you see --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Beleg because we were forced out from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were at Beleg as refugees, as you say in your statement, in other people's houses, did you see armoured vehicles that could be used for fighting?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night when we went to Beleg, there weren't any. The next the police came and searched; and then the next day in the evening the APCs came, the army, the police, and the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your statement you referred to a police officer beside who was inside the APCs, which is what I wanted to clarify. How many APCs or armoured vehicles did you see in Beleg?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many armoured vehicles, but I was separated from the rest of the population. I was made to stand against a wall, but there were many of them around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The armoured vehicles that you saw, who or which organisation did the armoured vehicles belong to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They belonged to the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you saw police there in Beleg. Why do you say they were police? Did you know any of them before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew them from before, especially from -- policemen from Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about the soldiers? How were you able to identify that these were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could identify them because they were wearing army clothes, and some of them were masked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "paramilitaries," what do you mean by that? You said you saw paramilitaries as well.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were paramilitaries as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Describe what you mean when you use the term "paramilitaries."

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I understand with paramilitaries is what -- people who had to do with the Army of Yugoslavia, people who had army clothes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. But you said that there were police, soldiers, and paramilitaries. What I'd like you to explain for us, if you can, is what is the distinction from -- according to your understanding, between the paramilitaries and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I understand, these were older than the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I refer to page 6 of the English version. This is the fourth full paragraph on that page. And it's the last paragraph on page 5 in which you describe where you had been asked by villagers in Beleg to go and speak with the police, to ask for permission to leave the village. And you were told to go to a basement. Now, did you go to the basement voluntarily? How were you told to go there, in what manner?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went there with some other elderly people to ask them to allow us to leave Beleg, but they told us to go to the basement. They took us to the basement and told us that, "In five minutes we will let you know." But they didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said later on, about an hour later, they brought the remainder of the villagers to the basement of that house?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is the first to lines on page 7, Your Honours, the fifth paragraph on the bottom of the page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said they brought the remainder of the villagers there. What I want to ask you is: How many other people did they bring to the house? You said you came from your town of Drenoc with 520 people from Drenoc and 37 from the neighbouring village of Slup. Now, when you were in the basement of the house, do you know about how many people were brought there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many can you estimate?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went to the basement, we found some persons there who had been taken there earlier than us. About 20-something people who had been close to the house, they were taken to the basement. Then during the day they brought several groups of people to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the police kept you in the basement and paramilitaries mistreated you and beat you from time to time, and also other people who were accommodated in the basement. Did you know some of these policemen before, and can you say where they were from?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this shelling started and we could hear the gun-fire, in the afternoon, when they took us out of the basement, they started to ill-treat us. And one of them was Zoran Gjurishiq from the police station in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you recognise any other police officer, or was he the only one you recognised?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the one that was leading the group of people. They had -- they were lined up. I recognised some other people from the police station, but I don't know their names. I also recognised some from the -- from Gjakova, but I don't know their names either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say that eventually yourself and the other villagers, who had sought refuge in Beleg, were put in a convoy and made to leave, "and there was an APC leading us out," according to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is page 10, first paragraph of the English statement and also page 9, first paragraph in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Whose APC it was-- when I say "who it belonged," I was associating it with which organisation APC that escorted the convoy of refugees out of Beleg?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many vehicles there, but one of them that I paid attention to was an army vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I want to be specific about is -- is the -- you said in your statement, "that APC's" - and there's an apostrophe in the English version - "were leading us out." And I understand there were military vehicles. Can I just ask you this question: How many vehicles escorted the people, or how many military or police vehicles escorted the people out of the town, of the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could count them, there were three APCs in front, Because I was the last one. My tractor was the last one to leave the village of Beleg, so that's what I could notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that one belonged to -- one in particular belonged to the army. To which organisation, if you know, did the other two APCs that escorted the people, the refugees, out of Beleg belong to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other two belonged to the police organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say how many refugees or villagers, who were Kosovar Albanians, left in that convoy?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy was made up of people from all the villages of the municipality of Decan. There were many people. They told us to go towards Decan, but then we were led towards Gjakova and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First, just if you can give me an approximate number, how many people were in the convoy that was led to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately hundreds of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, hundreds. Was it more than a thousand or less than a thousand?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than a thousand. The first time people escaped, there were thousands of people who left through the mountains and went to Albania. This time there were less than a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said there were 520 from your village, about 37 from Slup, that's about 550. Was it more or less --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- than this amount?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were more with -- including other villages, there were more than a thousand, but people from our village, they were about 520, 560 altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You arrived in Beleg on the 27th of March. What date -- what date did you leave Beleg with the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left Beleg on the 29th, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, from your statement, I see that you did not continue with the convoy to Albania, you jumped off because some of your family had been left behind and that you eventually left Kosovo to Albania with your family with a different group. What date, if you can remember, did you and your family leave Kosovo and go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that date very well. I left the convoy and went to look for my relatives, my family. On the 30th, I arrived at Isniq and joined my family. On the 30th, shelling started, so we had to leave en masse, all the inhabitants that were in Isniq at the time, and we had to go towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said, finally, that they took your documents and IDs in the Djakovica bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is the last sentence in the last paragraph of the statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was it who took your ID documents? Or I don't need you to tell me the persons individually, but did the persons belong to any organisation that you could identify? And I'm just talking about those who took the documents.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons who took our documents belonged to the police and the army. This happened at the sacred bridge or "Ura e Shejte" in Albanian, sometimes it's called "Ura e Drinit," the Drini bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I don't have anything further in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Mazrekaj, when you were describing the people who arrived in APCs, and you mentioned Zoran Gjurishiq as a person you recognised, in your statement, you also say that you recognise a policeman inside an APC who was Mushe Jakupi's son. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan -- oh, sorry, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will follow the following order: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Lazarevic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I'm one of the attorneys for the accused, Sreten Lukic. Today, I have some questions for you which I hope you can answer truthfully and concisely as possible. Therefore, I would ask you to pay close attention to what I am asking you -- and if you do not understand my question, please, let me now. Now, first of all sir, in your statement and here -- well, the past few days, you have said that in your home village of Drenovaca, there were a total number of six ethnic Serb families. Could you, please, tell me the total number of inhabitants in your village that these six ethnic Serb families encompassed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drenoc had altogether 2.000 inhabitants, approximately, and 200 houses, Albanian and Serb, all inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What portion of the 2.000 inhabitants were these six Serb families?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These six Serb families, two of them lived in the upper part of the village, while the rest were neighbours of mine. I can't tell you what percentage. I don't know how many they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did these six Serb families have some surnames that you recall or are familiar with, the six Serb families that were your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Zecevic, Jokic, these were neighbours. So in reality, in fact, these were three families of Zecevic and one Antic, four families, while the rest, Antic and Marijanovic, they lived in the upper part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, in your statement you mentioned a Serb family that fled your village for Serbia before the war broke out. Could you tell us when that family fled your village and what were the circumstances under which they had to flee.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly when they left. They left for economic reasons. I remember him very well. His name was Mija Antic. The others remained, they stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Now, in your direct examination you testified and clarified that portion of your statement where you said all the Serb families left, and you clarified that by saying all the Serb families left in 1998. Do you know what was the reason for all these Serb families to leave in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. I can't remember this. I think I said that during the offensive they went to their houses in Decan, to take shelter there, not that they left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say "during the offensive," we're talking about 1998 still. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was your village small enough so that you knew most of the persons in there by name?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Great. Now, am I correct that during the time that you left for Lumbarda and Pec, that is to say, prior to your -- that is to say, in 1998 when you say that 64 cannons surrounded your village. Am I correct that prior to that time the KLA or UCK had been operating within the Decani municipality and the surrounding area and had launched offensives against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. But it is not true that there were 68 cannons surrounding our village. They were positioned at a placed call Podi i Geshtenjane, and from that position the shelling was carried out towards our village and all the other villages belonging to the municipality of Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me take a few moments to highlight some of the KLA activities, to see what it is that you were aware of. Did you know about the widely publicised attack that took place on 25 April 1996, when three members of the KLA engaged in an armed attack against the Cakor Restaurant with armed rifles and grenades, killing three persons and wounding several others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, please. We really are going back in history now, Mr. Ivetic. The crucial thing is what were the factors that might have justified the presence of the army in this sort of arrangement or, indeed, the police at the time that is relevant, which is 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- two years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the 1996 incident is important because that is, based upon my research, when the turning point came between the relations between local Serbs and local Albanians in the area, which is why I actually hadn't finished the question, which was going to ask if that was the turning point when the relations soured or changed somewhat. Since in his statement he identifies that the relationships between Serbs and Albanians were fine, but then all of a sudden the Serbs are leaving and he doesn't have a date for that information in his statement. So I believe that I'm trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, that explains a basis for it. On you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- well, let me start from the beginning just so there's no confusion, sir. Did you know about an event that occurred on 25 April 1996 when three members of the KLA, and specifically two members of the -- two local residents, Agron Tolaj and Arif Vokshi, engaged in an armed attack upon the Cakor Restaurant, killing three persons and wounding several others. Do you recall that incident, and do you recall whether the relationship between the local Serbs and Albanians in the municipality, and in particular in your village, changed after that event?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall this at all. Whilst regarding the relationship, I can say here that we had a good relationship with the -- especially the Montenegrin minority that lived there. But it is also true that relationships were worsened, were exacerbated a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was Agron Tolaj from your village of Drenovac, was he one of the Tolaj families that lived in Drenovac?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not come from Drenoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you -- and let's move now to 1998, and in particular I'd like to talk right now about June of 1998. Do you recall a series of coordinated attacks that occurred over several days in June of 1998, wherein Serbian family residences in 18 villages of mixed ethnicity in the Decani municipality were attacked by the KLA, leading to the mass exodus of all 295 Serb families from these villages?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was personally involved in the education process and had no connection at all with the KLA or their attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, wasn't -- wasn't this a widely publicised occurrence that people talked about, heard about, in June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you recall whether the -- whether there was much tension, as you called it, I believe, exacerbated tension or exacerbated relationships after June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, questions are not confined to your statement. I think I explained at the beginning that the reason for you being here is so that you can be asked about things that go beyond your statement, among other reasons; and there's no reason why these questions should not be asked. Now, it's not being suggested at the moment that you have any connection with the KLA. What you're being asked about are matters which counsel claims were within public knowledge, and you as an informed person in the area are someone that counsel feels might be able to tell us if this was generally speaking the situation in the area. So it would help us if you could approach it on that basis and do our best to give us as much information as you have from your general knowledge of the situation at the time. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, sir, I had asked you whether what you had described as exacerbated relationships between the Serbs and the Albanians, I'd like to ask you if that -- if you recall whether that took place or worsened after June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did after June 1998. Whilst regarding the relationship within the is village with the Montenegrins that lived there, the relationship stayed normal at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's get back to your village for a second. Based on your knowledge and information, was there any KLA activity in your home village; that is to say, either an active KLA presence, KLA members that hailed from your village, or active material support of the KLA by persons in your village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no KLA presence in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about weapons, was anyone in your village armed either in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, with the exception of the two local policemen who bore weaponry, given that they were armed by the police at Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as your assertions that there was no KLA presence and no armaments in the village, are you absolutely certain about that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fairly certain for the duration of the time I was there, and I cannot speak of the time after we left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I take it then that you did not have any family members that were affiliated with the KLA or engaged in smuggling arms from the Republic of Albania?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with Rram Mazrekaj, born in 1967, from the village of Drenovac, a village that you have said had a population of 2.000 persons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him very well. He's my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I suppose that you are not familiar with his open -- openly admitted membership in the KLA, and his boasting of the killing of Selaji Istrefa [phoen] and the smuggling of weapons from Albania to further the KLA cause?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rram, regarding this issue, never said that one, because he was arrested at Isniq when he was going from that village to another village. He was also arrested on another occasion, as he was making his way to Albania somewhere. But he was arrested up on the mountains on the Plava region; and alongside a number of other people, he was sent to jail and made to serve a long sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And his sentence was for smuggling arms from Albania, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was caught on his way to Montenegro up in the mountains, alongside other people. And he -- he alongside the other of his friends was given a 15-year-long jail sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is the source of this voluntary statement given by Rram Mazrekaj to the OTP or some other source?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's some other source. I'm trying to track down Rram Mazrekaj's statement. I had found another source that was an OTP statement, talking about meeting Mr. Mazrekaj in the jail. But I am about to move on to other individuals for whom I do have some documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you sure that the activities of the KLA within your home village didn't have anything to do with the Serbs and the Montenegrins leaving that village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was absolutely no connection between KLA activities and the Serbs leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall, back in 1998 again, in May and June of that year that the Pec-Djakovica road was in fact completely blocked by the UCK/KLA, to such an extent that all normal traffic had to pass across Montenegro to get to and from Pristina from Pec?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that road is very near to your village. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the road that links Gjakova and Decani. It's not too far from my village, about a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about some specific persons from your village, residents of Drenovac in the Decani municipality. Do you know any of the following persons: Zek Mazrekaj, Dukaj, Nitaj, Baqaj Milanim, Bajram Alaj, Dukaj Halil, Dukaj Vlaznim, Nitaj Gzim, Baqaj Bashkim, or Ibir Alaj, do you know any of these persons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know all of these persons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know all of these people who come from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you be surprised to learn that in 1998 a staff headquarters of the UCK or KLA was formed in your village headed by Dukaj Halil and including Dukaj Vlaznim, Nitaj Gzim, and Baqaj Bashkim?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this headquarters was formed. I wasn't there. I was staying with my ill father for a number of days in Peje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, were you in your home village of Drenovac in April of 1998 at any time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you if you recall -- first of all, who is Zek Mazrekaj?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two Zekas there, and I don't know whether you're working for the senior or the junior of the Zekajs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were they related to you or were they neighbours of yours, both of them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you be surprised to find out that in April of 1998 Zek Mazrekaj, Dukaj, Nitaj, Baqaj Milanim and Bajram Alaj brought 50 automatic rifles from Albania to your village for the use of the UCK detachment stationed there? Would you be surprised or did you already know that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fact doesn't surprise me, but I know that during this time, Zek Mazrekaj was working in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Both of the Zek Mazrekajs?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The senior of them died, and the junior was working in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what about Tahir Alaj, the son of Rexhep, Dukaj Bajram, Abdullah Mazrekaj, and Sami Mazrekaj, I take it you know these individuals as well, since they also hail from Drenovac?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They don't come from Drenoc. There are Mazrekajs in Prilep, Sllup, and Voksh. They don't come from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So then I take it that you deny the fact that those four KLA fighters died in your village in the course of battles between the UCK and the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean exactly? Who was killed in my village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when you repeat the question, Mr. Ivetic, could we also have a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe we're still talking about 1998, Your Honour, specifically in March and April of 1998. And the names are Tahir Alaj, the son of Rexhep; Dukaj Bajram; Abdullah Mazrekaj; and Sami Mazrekaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in fact these persons died in your village of Drenovac in March and/or April of 1998 when they were battling as members of the UCK against Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tahir Alaj was an elderly man who I knew very well. He died going from his own house towards the Skola Bajramit [phoen] and he didn't belong to the KLA at all. The other three, and their names are not correct, did not come from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, how did he die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tahir was found dead in the vicinity of our school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I don't know what he was killed from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you know if it was from natural causes or a violent death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Violence. It wasn't a natural death. He died as a result of violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to place Exhibit 6D103 on e-court, the statement of Ibir Alaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One of the individuals you indicated that you recognised as being from your village. Now, while we're waiting for that come up, sir, I only have the document in Serbian and in English, so I'm going to have to read the relevant portions of it to you to pose questions about your co-villagers and their activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just make an inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to this statement. If it was received from the OTP, I just ask because I'm trying to check if the person named here, who gave the statement, might well be protected in another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This document was received from the OTP, so perhaps we should maybe go into closed session just to be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm making inquiries now because I think perhaps we should -- we could redact the name of the giver of the statement and not use it, if it's not necessary, while the checks are being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've got no problem with that, going into private session as well or the less restrictive of the two sessions, if -- at this point, if that is a concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll briefly go into private session to just consider this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, what is the basis for your intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In a converse case to this where members of the KLA Kosovo Albanian leadership are prosecuted, there are huge security issues from the witnesses. If this was a statement that was taken from disclosure by the OTP, it might well be that this is a protected witness so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And would that not be clear from the statement that you give to the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it would not be clear from this statement. This statement is a statement that apparently was taken by the local Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But first of all we don't know if this person is a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Secondly, you're not stating any basis for claiming that this name should not be in the public domain and that this trial should be held partly in private to consider it. So what is the basis on which that we can redact part of the transcript or go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not asking for private session. I'm just asking that simply the name be redacted where it was used once, while the checks are made and, if necessary, not be used. If I discover the person is not a witness, then the order to redact could be reversed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what we'll do in this instance is redact that one reference. Mr. Ivetic, please don't use the name, if you can avoid it, but draw it to my attention if it is necessary raise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours, and the exhibits have his name on there so maybe we should tender them under seal at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you have hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do I have hard copy, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the witness could have a trial -- if you're putting the exhibit to the witness, then to so avoid it appearing on the screen, you would need to give him a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe he speaks the language of either of the hard copies, so that's not an issue. To be quite frank, I don't think it needs to be on the screen at all, if that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I ask him if he speaks Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe his witness statement said he did not -- oh, he does. I could give him a hard copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering if we can have some clarification of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's. Can we go back into open session first of all, or do you need to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I think open session is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Stamp was talking about danger these witnesses might be involved in with regard to cases against KLA members. I assume he's talking about danger they might face by testifying in any way that would harm the KLA, if that's correct. I think it's important to know that, because it could impact this case, too, if that's a situation that prevails.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I wasn't referring to anything. In almost any case we have here, there are witnesses who are -- who have to be protected, especially if they say things where certain persons who are charged are named. If you look at this statement, you'll see that certain persons who are charged are named in this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is an issue we can't explore in the context of this debate at the moment. You know that the Bench have reservations about having any part of the trial in private or redacting references that have been made, but out of an abundance of caution that's been done on this instance. And we shall now proceed in open session with the cross-examination of the witness. And I remind you, Mr. Ivetic, that you have to strike a balance in cross-examination between the extent to which you present the Defence case and the extent to which you cross-examine the witness on the Prosecution case, and you must be getting near exhaustion of the time that might be available for the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, first of all, do you -- your written statement to the OTP says that you speak Serbian. Does that include the fact that you're able to read Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do read Serbian; however, I'm not fully competent to read this piece of paper. I haven't been called here on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Then I think I will read in English and allow the translators to translate into Albanian then for the limited few questions that I have on this before moving on to the other topics. Now, sir, this statement from the individual whom we will not name, who hails from the village of Drenovac, in this statement he says that he had to return to Drenovac in March of 1998 from where he was studying, precisely because his mother had to flee the village to escape fighting between the UCK/KLA and the Serb police. Now, isn't it true that in March of 1998 not only was there a UCK/KLA presence in your village, but that they mounted attacks from within the village and engaged in fierce battles with the local police, so intense that the villagers had to flee the village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember this. There were -- there was sporadic fighting, but I am not aware of this case of Ibir Alaj, even though I know him. I have never ever talked to him or ever held a meeting with him from that day onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Until this stage of the evidence is over, we will be in private session, and that part will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and, Your Honours, I think I will still refer to the individual without using his name for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but it hasn't prevented the witness using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this statement goes on to say at page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S that: "It is known to me that the first arms in the village of Drenovac arrived during April 1998 in a manner by which five persons travelled to RA" -- Interpreter's Note: Republic of Albania -- "from where they brought three horse-loads to the village consisting of approximately 50 AP" -- Interpreter's Note: Automatic Rifles. "This group is made up of Zek Mazrekaj, Dukaj, Binak, Dem Nitaj, Baqaj Milanim, and Bajram Alaj. The arms were stored in the houses of the commander of the DTG staff in Drenovac, Dukaj Halil. Further weapons were later brought to the village, but since I was at the time in Prizren, I am not aware who brought them or the quantities." Now, sir, does this refresh your recollection as to the fact that a terrorist cell of the UCK was in fact in your village and that it was armed in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any terrorist base in the -- in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you know any of these individuals that we have named as participating in the arming --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I've just been advised that the name is not a name of a protected witness, and therefore the need for the redaction and private session doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, return to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that the position in relation to the name mentioned has been clarified, the Chamber revokes the redactions of the two passages in the transcript and revokes the two private session parts of the evidence, and we shall proceed further in open session, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I only have about two or three questions on this. And I will be moving on, I believe, to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I believe I had asked you if you knew any of the individuals in March and April of 1998 that were named as either being part of the UCK staff in Drenovac or for bringing weapons to Drenovac. Did you see any of them during that time-period? Did you socialise with them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was friends with them. I went to school with them, but what you're saying is not believable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, it's not what I'm saying; it's what the gentleman from your village is saying. And I have just one more question relating to that statement. Now, in the statement he identifies specifically Tahir Rexhep Alaj, Mazrekaj Abdullah, Mazrekaj Sami, and Dukaj Bajram as members of the armed group in your village that died in battles with the Serbian authorities. These are the individuals you said that you did not recognise before. Does that refresh your recollection as to whether, in fact, they were in your village at some point in time, either in March or in April of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tahir Alaj was -- he was killed in our village. The other ones, I don't know them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, you identified some -- some skirmishes from time to time and activity in the area. I'd like to find out where exactly the KLA activity was. Mr. Alaj identifies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just make it clear to you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will impose a limit on this cross-examination, so please be careful about what you're doing in relation to the extent you are exploring the case that you yourself can advance yourself later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, Your Honours, I will -- that was my last question on 1998, but I will move to 1999 in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you described two local Albanians from your village that you say collaborated with the Serbian government. How were Albanians who chose not to fight against their state viewed by the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were two brothers, Shaban and Ali, Haxhi, Kadrijaj. Shaban is about 60 years old, Ali 58. They were local policemen in our village. There were other villages who had local policemen, but I'm speaking here about my village. And we had good relations with them, but they collaborated with the Serbian police and were armed all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did they have uniforms different from the regular police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe they had the uniforms at home, but they were in plain clothes when they went out in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you -- prior to March of 1999, am I correct that from -- when you returned in 1998 to your village to that point, despite the constant presence and attacks of the KLA, that you did not have any problems from the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we returned to the village the second time, we found a check-point in the village. They asked us to give them our IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's already in your statement. Apart from that, did you have any encounters or problems with the police?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time OSCE came, we did not have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk about when you left your village. You've already identified the source of your comments to your local -- to the rest of your villagers that they were going to be separating the men and the women, and we see that that was an invention of yours. You did not have any knowledge -- no one had threatened to separate the men from the women at the check-point or elsewhere. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct what I said, and that happened later in Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, when you passed Beleg, did you go through the village of Prilep and did you pass by any policemen in Prilep?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We passed through the northern part of Prilep, through the fields and pathways, and we got to Beleg. The policemen, we did not see them in Beleg, but they were stationed around the hills in Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in March -- March 28th, while you were in Beleg at the home of Zenel Vishaj, you heard shooting. And when you went outside, did you see anyone shooting upon the police?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the house of Zenel Vishaj with Qazim Hulaj and a friend from Prilep. We heard the gun-fire and we went out. Qazim left. He went down the garden, and he was killed. I did not see him, but I learned later that he was killed. And then I did not leave the house any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you if you had seen anyone shooting upon the police; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone shooting on the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the fact that on that day and the next day there was a fierce gun-fighting in nearby Pozar between members of the UCK and the Serbian police in which, on a total, there were two policemen killed and 15 policemen wounded on that two-day period, just in that one village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Gjurishiq told me that in Beleg, at the check-point. He told me, Mr. Teacher, your pupils have killed us in Pozhar and they won't allow us to go and get the killed. This is what I heard from Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct that prior to the arrival of the police in Beleg, that UCK personnel or armed Albanians were in Beleg as well?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see any KLA in Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I have just a handful of questions left, so I'd like to go through them quickly. First of all, in what house was your sister's husband Daut Alickaj located in Beleg?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house of Adem Vishaj. We were together at that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to ask you about this Zoran Gjurishiq. What type of uniform did he have on that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regular police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe that uniform, paying attention to any colours or anything on the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the regular blue colour of the police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see anything else on the uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I did not go close to him. I was not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, based upon what he told you and the way he acted, did you believe that he was angry over the wounded and killed police that had died at the hands of the KLA and whose bodies the KLA was preventing them from going to recover? Do you believe that he was angry that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. He knows that. I'm not a psychologist to see or to notice whether he was angry or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were his conversations with you calm?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand you. You mean the policemen? No, they talked to me in a brutal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you -- in your statement you say that they were drinking. Were they drinking during that period of time, these persons that were there in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they detained us and took us to the second floor, downstairs they continued to drink and eat and all the other ceremonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let me ask you about the APCs. First of all, could you describe just the APCs that you identify as being police APCs. Could you tell us a little bit about the colour, the number and location of the doors, and any markings on those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the vehicles from far away. They were not close to where we were, but I know that they were blue, the police colour. It was easy to distinguish them. I can distinguish the army colour and the other colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see any markings?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it was not close; it was far.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see how many doors were on the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't because we were surrounded by police and army soldiers in that yard or garden where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now, when you went to Isniq to be with your family and then decided to leave for Albania, am I correct that at that point in time there was no policeman present who ordered you or otherwise told you to go to Albania, were there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a very large group of people in Isniq from various villages, and shelling started from Strellc, so from the western part of Isniq, and from Podi i Geshtenjane. So the villagers said we had to leave, and all of us took the way towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there were no policemen present at that time in the village when the villagers told you to leave and when you left for Albania?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was lying down in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mazrekaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I pass to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I inquire how much time is left for the rest of us to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By my count, 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would reckon a bit more than that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Roughly 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's way more than enough, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, I just have some very, very brief questions for you, and I think we can finish maybe even by the time of the break. When you first went to Beleg, you say that the local people there told you that you should stay there, because 18 Serb soldiers had been killed and the roads were blocked. I take it they told you those soldiers were killed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were normal people. They were frightened, and they had heard that the road to Isniq had been sealed off. So it would be better for us to stay there that night until the next day, so that we would see what would go -- what would happen the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear the question that I asked you? I asked you about whether the soldiers were killed by the KLA. Did you hear that question?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of fighting there was there, because I was in Beleg and that village was far from Beleg; Pozhar was far from Beleg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, you were told 18 Serb soldiers had been killed. Who did you understand had killed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard from the villagers that they were killed in a confrontation with the KLA. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to skip now to the time when you were leaving the country at this bridge where you say that the people who took your documents were the police and the army. Did you hand over any documents that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day I was on the tractor. The tractor was covered --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is very simple: Did you hand over any documents that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any documents on me, so I didn't hand anything over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So nobody, police or army, took documents from you, did they?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took documents from other people who were with me on the same tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you say "they did," were those documents handed to an army person or a police person?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents were given to a police person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In questioning by Mr. Ivetic about KLA activity in your village, you basically told Mr. Ivetic that there were no weapons, that there were no KLA, that there were no armaments in your village. So would it be fair to say that what happened in your village didn't have anything to do with any armed conflict that might have been going on between the Serbian forces and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware about these things, whether there were arms in my village or whether there was KLA. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We could have probably saved some time if you've told us that much earlier. I just have one -- well, I have two more questions. When you were in Isniq, you say the shelling started. When you say "shelling," what are you talking about? What do you mean shelling?"

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Irzniq or Isniq? Which of the villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm now confused. Which one were you in that you left when the shelling started? That's the one that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time, we were in Isniq and not Irzniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Isniq, what are you talking about when you say "shelling started?"? What do you mean "shelling started?"

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they started to shell the villages. They started to shell Isniq as well, so we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What do you mean "to shell"?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, shelling with cannons, they know, with artillery, they know what they did. The aim was to destroy the village and us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where was this artillery that was firing at that village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier they were in Zalli i Strelcit and Podi i Geshtenjane. These were the main points from where they were shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the shells were landing in this village where you were?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were shells that came, ended up in our village and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They the houses in the village, did they?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how many people were killed by that shelling in Isniq, where you were, before you left? How many people were killed from those shells?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Isniq, but people were killed in Strellc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Isniq. You said there because the shelling started, you had to leave. How many people were killed by that shelling that you say was hitting that village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were many people there, and everybody was trying to find some vehicle and get prepared to go towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, weren't people, after you left there, talking about their friend and relatives that didn't leave the village because they'd been hit by shells? Wasn't there talk about that? Or isn't it the case that there simply was no shelling and nobody was injured there or hurt?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. After we left the village, I'm not aware of how many people remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. One final question then. Although you didn't say anything about it in your statement to the OTP - which you, I know, had occasion to review and determine whether it was correct or not - you said in a separate conversation with members of the OTP that you saw members of the army in the village of Beleg when you were there. The question I have for you is this: If it is later shown in this case that there were no army members present in Beleg at that time, then what would you tell us -- who would you tell us that these people are that you thought must have been army members? Who would they be then if they couldn't have been army?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Objection. The question seems to invite speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to me to be an appropriate question, Mr. Ackerman. I understand why you're asking it, but I don't think it's either necessary or appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two administrative matters I want to deal with just now. My attention's been drawn this morning to an application, a joint Defence -- objection, rather, to the trial schedule for the week commencing the week of the 27th of November. If we alter the actual the actual projected schedule from half day to some other arrangement, then there will be a scheduling order issued. All that has happened is that there has been included in the court programme the potential for sitting longer than simply half a day during that week and I think one other week in December. I can tell you that under no circumstances will we in these two weeks, if we extend the hours, extend them to six hours, nor will we extend them in a way that will make it unreasonable -- well, will make it unreasonably difficult for the parties to continue with their preparation. That's exactly what we said we would do in the previous order, and there is no intention to change that. I'm sorry if a false impression has been created, because in the administrations court schedule allocation has been given. So I would invite the Defence to withdraw that application, that notice; it is pointless in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the permission of my colleagues we will withdraw it, and I'm sorry if there was a misunderstanding. I thought we could rely on those schedules that Ms. Ameerali sends us to us occasionally. I thought they were done with the Court's approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But where we change from the normal routine, we will issue a scheduling order and you should await that or, alternatively, make inquiry of Mr. Dawson if you're concerned about anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I appreciate that very much and that will be the case in the future and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not at all. I understand why it's happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just want to be clear that we're not going back on what we said before and we have no intention of doing that. Obviously, if unexpected events arise and we were to alert you to the possibility and give you a chance to comment if we were going to change what we had said in the past. The second is this. There is an application for an alternation to protective measures for a witness that the Prosecution seek to identify as K85. In view of the schedule, it will be necessary to deal with that application at some stage today. I alert the Defence to that so that someone can be in a position to respond. But I also want to make it clear that the Bench -- I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you're in the middle of talking about that, Your Honour, and I didn't want to interrupt you, but I think Mr. O'Sullivan is working on that and will be here after the break and will be prepared to address that issue. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I do want to say, however, that this practice of raising these matters at the last minute is unacceptable to the Chamber. I have ad nauseam commented on the failure of the Prosecution to present things to us in an orderly way. This is another example. If there is going to be delay in making final arrangements with witnesses for the presentation of their evidence, applications of this nature are going to come to the Tribunal -- to the Trial Chamber in circumstances where they are under pressure to make a decision, and that's quite inappropriate. These applications must be directed to us in time to enable the Defence to respond in the usual way. In future, if this happens, the witness will have to be postponed until the ordinary course is followed, unless there is good cause for the application coming at the last minute. And the fact that the Prosecution have chosen not to speak to the witness until the last minute will not be viewed by the Trial Chamber as good cause. We will, however, deal with this particular one, since it's only now that we are making clear the course that we will follow in the future. We'll adjourn now and resume at five minutes to 11.00. We have to have a break now, Mr. Mazrekaj. The usher will show you where to wait for the next 20 minutes or so. If you would kindly go with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the delayed start. I didn't realise that the redactions would cause a longer period for the changeover of tapes at the interval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some questions, Your Honour, but I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mazrekaj. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney-at-law, counsel for General Lazarevic. In your first statement from February 2000, you didn't mention the fact that some VJ members were in Beleg in March 1998 [as interpreted] and you mentioned that for the first time on the 30th of October, 2006. As regards that, I wanted to know the following: You saw VJ members in Beleg in their vehicles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1998, but in 1999. In March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I believe I said in March 1999. There may have been an error in the transcript. You saw VJ members in Beleg in March 1999 in their vehicles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you weren't able to notice any details of the uniform as regard colour or insignia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able, but at -- Mushe Jakupi was wearing an army uniform -- Jakupi's son.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were also familiar with the fact that Mushe Jakupi was a member of the police, of the local police force?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't Mushe himself, it was Mushe Jakupi's sons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, let's be clear about this. The person you recognised as Mushe Jakupi's son, you've just described as wearing an army uniform. In your statement, you said that you recognised him as a policeman. Could you clarify that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two sons of Mushe Jakupi, one had an army uniform, the other one had a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have to correct the transcript. Did you know that both of his sons were members of the local security force?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know whether they were members of the local police or army, but I know them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The one son of Mushe Jakupi, which as you claim wore a military uniform, can you explain what his uniform looked like.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual uniform that the army wore, the one that the VJ had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, I didn't serve my military term. Could you please assist me and describe for me the way the uniform looked like.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not interested in whether you served your military service, but I'm fully aware of what a military uniform looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mazrekaj. I would kindly ask you to share your knowledge with us. Please describe that uniform for us.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking me to do, if you don't know what the uniform looks like. But I know very well what a police or military uniform looks like. I know what the VJ army wore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, could you give us just a general description, please, of that uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to describe it. This appears absurd to me to be asked to describe what the military uniform looks like when even little children know what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be that colour would help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not wearing -- I can't see anything that looks that colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Different branches of armed forces often have different uniforms, and it is a reasonable line of inquiry for counsel to ask you if you can help by describing the uniform in any way. You don't feel you can give us any assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was able to tell what an army person or a police person wore. There were only those two uniforms that were around; there wasn't a third one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since you were unable to extract an answer, I will not press this any further. I will just ask Mr. Mazrekaj to tell me whether he would be unable to describe the difference between the military and the police vehicles as well, or rather, can he provide that description for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were different. The army vehicles had their own colour and police vehicles were blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say the military vehicles had their own colour. What colour was that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were they monochrome grey? When you say "grey," it was a solid colour, I guess?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't mixed up at all. It was what I call the army colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you see any symbols on the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I wasn't too close and able to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I believe they had wheels, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were somewhere on a hill, a bit in a courtyard, and there were people mounted on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, Mr. Mazrekaj, you are telling us that you couldn't see any details on the vehicles because they were far away and it's a hilly terrain.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a hilly terrain, but we were very able to see the people mounted on them. And they the targets trained on us and I was able to distinguish the colours very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say they trained their weapons on you, what sort of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guns, they were all trained on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, I have just one more question for you. If I understood properly, you were at the rear of the column which set out from Beleg. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And it comprised some 1.000 people, as you stated today?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How long was it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit more than that. It went through a flat road in the direction of Carrabreg; however, I was unable to measure it. I didn't have a tape measure on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, I'm not asking you to be precise, but as a geography teacher I believe you can navigate in space. So can you tell us, was it two 2 kilometres long?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy was about one and a half kilometres, a bit longer perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And as far as I understand, Mr. Mazrekaj, before the column reached Djakovica you abandoned the column; you jumped off and left?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't part of the convoy. I got off at the bridge called Bridge of Bajram Hasani. That's not part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You separated together with your tractor, or did you go on foot?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where did you go with your tractor?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was on my own. Someone else was driving the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you left the column, you yourself riding on your tractor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. A girl was driving the tractor, whilst I was moving on foot through the fields. I was not with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Mazrekaj, you were not able to see the vehicles at the front of the column, which is contrary to what you stated today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. The [indiscernible] were in the direction of Beleg and we moved towards Beleg and not on the occasion when we went towards Gjakova and then towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Mazrekaj, I'm asking you about the column which set out for Beleg. In your statement, on the last page, you stated, on the way to Decani, I realised we were being sent to Djakovica.
