When the vehicles slowed down, I jumped off my tractor, whilst now we are receiving a completely new piece of information. I would be interested to find out which is correct.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we set off from Beleg, we headed towards Decan; however, at Carrabreg, our direction was changed and we were veered towards Gjakova. So when we arrived at the bridge, there was a lorry and a column of tractors, and I got off but they continued their route towards Gjakova. But this was the journey from Beleg. I think -- and it includes those people who went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you were at the rear of the column, which was almost 2 kilometres long, you couldn't see who was at the front - am I not correct in asserting that - and then you also abandoned the column?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the column when the column reached the main road towards Gjakova. There was a big lorry of the police. And when the police and Male Vishaj's son was driving the lorry with women on board and they left, that was the point where I was able to notice how long this convoy was and the number of vehicles in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mazrekaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mazrekaj, you said at one point in that evidence that you had left the tractor and you were on foot going through the fields and a girl drove the tractor. Who was the girl?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The girl came from my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was that when you were in the convoy from Beleg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mazrekaj, my name is Tomislav Visnjic, counsel for General Ojdanic. I have a few questions for you. Mr. Mazrekaj, is it correct that the village of Istinic is some 5 kilometres away from your village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about 5 kilometres and a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Sinanaj Brahim Beta [phoen], who owned a shop in Istinic or in one of the surrounding locations?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 3D99, page 2 prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know of such a person?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard that there are Betas in Isniq. I do not know this person in particular, but I am aware that there are Betas in Isniq.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the position's been clarified, Mr. Visnjic, but Istinic, as you pronounce, is the same place as Isniq. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Isniq and Irzniq are two different places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But your interest, Mr. Visnjic, is in the village which in Albanian is called Isniq. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm still waiting for the interpretation. I believe Istinic and Isniq are the two names for that same location; one name is in Albanian, the other in Serbian. Since we had the confusion a minute ago about Irzniq and Isniq, I intentionally used this Serb name so as to make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Mehaj Alija, who is also from Isniq?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How about a Islamaj Islam?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Mazrekaj, that in February 1999, on several occasions, some uniformed KLA members visited several families in the area of Istinic and threatened to kill them because of the following reasons: Because they organised the handing over of weapons in September 1998, because they cooperated with the police, and because they didn't support the KLA, they didn't send any of their family members to the KLA. Are you familiar with any of the incidents that took place in Istinic in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, please, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Mazrekaj, you told us yesterday that you had been appointed or elected a sort of supervisor in your village. Did no one draw to your attention that uniformed KLA members had been or had visited them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No one did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mazrekaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like Defence Exhibit 3D99, page 6, to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that a neighbouring village, Locane, is about 1 kilometre away from your village, your village of Drenovac?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably less than 1 kilometre. We're adjacent villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You told us that there were no Serb families in your village in March 1999. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left the village and went and occupied flats in Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: They left before March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they left. Some of them left earlier, some later. And from time to time they came back to look after their houses, the animals they'd left behind, the livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And are you aware, Mr. Mazrekaj, that in the village of Locane, families Antic, Simic, Popovic, Denicevic, and Mijatovic left the village on the 22nd March, 1999, because they were ordered by KLA soldiers to do so?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know these families, almost all of them. I do not know exactly when they left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll remind you then. They left on the 22nd of March, 1999. Does that help you any?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date they left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Maybe you will be assisted by this: Their houses were burned down on the 24th and 25th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Lloqan, so I'm not aware of the date when the houses were burned, and that includes Albanian and Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were you in your village on the 24th and 25th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Didn't you see any smoke coming from the neighbouring village, which was less than a kilometre away?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our village is a bit elongated towards the rear part of that village, so I wasn't too close to be able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You told us you were the senior in the village. Did nobody tell you of the other villages? Did anybody tell you the news that 500 or 800 metres away from your village houses were burning?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because at that time our movement was restricted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, is it your evidence today that you saw nothing because you know that in Locane village, in the period from at least the 22nd of March until the 25th of March, there were KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about a presence. From the 27th, when we left the village, we went to Beleg. And the two or three days before that, I did not have any information about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, when did you first learn that Serb houses in Locane village had been burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never heard this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness. I would just like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, if you did feel that you wanted to make use of a further seven or eight minutes, that would be open to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm fine with the cross I completed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence and for assisting us. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and I wish you success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, does Mr. Zogaj now return?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I think the next witness is Shefqet Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While he's on his way, Your Honour, can I just step out briefly for a personal break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated. You gave evidence earlier in the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And at that stage you make a solemn declaration to speak the truth. That declaration continues to apply to your evidence today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you will now be cross-examined by Defence counsel, and I will ascertain first of all the order in which that will take place. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. First will be General Pavkovic, General Lukic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to take up a great deal of your time. You've made several statements over the course of your dealings with the Office of the Prosecutor I see. And one thing that has struck me about at least portions of your statements is that they have a kind of a journalistic flare to them, which probably comports with your experience as a journalist. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can give you an example. For instance, in your statement of April of 1999, in paragraph 2, you're talking about on the 20th of March of 1999 when you were in Suva Reka for the last time. You said: "The town was empty of people." You only found seven people from one end to the other; and then you say: "There was great fear about." And that's what I mean by kind of journalistic flair. The only people who could have had fear, I suppose, were those seven people that were left in the village; correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify something here, please. On the 20th of March, 1999, this was the day when the OSCE mission withdrew from Suhareke. In Suhareke, you could see only some Serb civilian vehicles. The town was completely empty, and there was no movement of the population. There was nobody in town. Some of the shops were open, but there were no people. And when we speak about Suhareke, after OSCE left, this was the time when the Serb paramilitary, army, and police forces started their operations in the direction of the village of Rreshtan. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is all in your statement, which is part of the evidence, and I think it was unnecessary for you to tell us all that stuff that was in there. The thing I found kind of is striking was - and you just emphasised it - the town was basically empty; and yet you said there was great fear about. All I was suggesting was the only people who could have been afraid, I guess, were those seven Serbs, apparently, that were left there.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To clarify this, where were the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These people were moving in the streets of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say there was seven people around, but there were the rest of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we say "seven people," these were seven Serb persons moving about. While in the centre of the Council for the Protection of Human Rights, they had an office in Suhareke, there were only four or five people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of that same statement is a bit unclear to me. You talked about leaving Suva Reka and going in the direction of the village of Pecane. You walked through the main road that passed through Restane and Studencane on the way to Orahovac. You saw a convoy. You say there was a Serbian police check-point at Restane, and then you say: "The other areas were controlled by the UCK." Now, what other areas was it you're referring to that were controlled by the UCK?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add something here. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you don't add something. Answer my question. What other areas were controlled by the UCK?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot respond to your question without clarifying something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't agree with that, Mr. Zogaj. You can answer that question; and then, if clarification is sought, one of us will seek it. But you say the other areas were controlled by the UCK. Please tell us what other areas you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During this period, the areas controlled by the KLA were: Decan, Semetisht, Doberdolan, Pagarusha, Samadrazhe, and some other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, I want to be clear what you mean in your statement, going back to the previous issue. Your statement says: "I only found a few people in the town. I only found seven from one end to the other. I saw nothing but police cars that were without licence plates. All the cars belonging to the civilian population, none of them were moving. There was great fear about." Where were the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Albanian population was inside their own houses, in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to paragraph 11 now. That's on page 4 where you say this: "A large convoy of Serbian police, military, and paramilitaries had reached Malisheve from the direction of Orllat consisting of 40 heavy military vehicles. I saw this from the hill at Banja." And I want to ask you about this convoy. When was this that you saw this? Can you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said from the hill of Orllat. I said from the district of Malisheve, from the village of Ajkali [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there may be an interpretation problem here; let me see if we can clear it up. Your statement says that this convoy had reached Malisheve from the direction of Orllat, O-r-l-l-a-t, and that you saw it from a hill at Banja. Now, is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. When did this happen? When did you see this?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on the 28th of March, 1999, 27th and 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you're on this hill at Banja and you see this convoy arrive. You saw it arrive on the 27th and the 28th? It arrived on two days?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it's been a long time. Now I think it was the 28th of March when the convoy of the police and paramilitary arrived there, and they started to shell in the direction of the villages, Banja, Dragobil, Senik, Lladroc. And on the same day, a whole family suffered from the shelling and Velime Begaj was killed; she died.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The thing I want to suggest to you is that if you don't remember a date or something like that, I'd much prefer you to tell me you don't remember than to sort of guess what day it might have been. You can say it could have been the 27th or the 28th, I'm not sure. But you don't have to give me a date just because I ask for one if you don't remember. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us how you distinguished between police, military, and paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And could you describe those specifically for each of the three?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I earlier brought some photographs of the Serbian police here, together with their tanks. The police wear blue; the Serb army wear green, camouflage; while the paramilitary uniforms are various. They were wearing black uniforms, they had bandannas on their heads and on their necks. Some of them had shaven heads. Some others wore big beards. Isn't this real? We also have photographs of all of these. If you don't, I have the photographs here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't challenging anything. I was just asking you to tell us on what you base those conclusions, and you did so, and I appreciate it. Thank you. Paragraph 13 of your statement which begins on page 4 and continues over to page 5, there's some confusing language there that I don't really understand. What you say - and I don't know if I can put you in the scene or not, but you'll remember it when I talk about it - "I had only moved about a metre down the lane when two Serbian soldiers and paramilitaries came wearing black uniforms and scarves around their necks. They pulled me out of the car." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. This happened on the 1st of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what I want to ask you about that is: These two Serbian soldiers and paramilitaries, were they soldiers, were they paramilitaries, were they both? If they were wearing black uniforms and scarves, they would be what you describe as paramilitaries. I just don't understand. Where did the "Serbian soldiers" language come from?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian politics never understands the things that have really happened. On the 1st of April, I was pulled out of my car by two Serb policemen, and I was taken to the basement of my house. I was beaten up there, robbed, and they hit me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please stop. You're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you about these two Serbian soldiers and paramilitaries that came wearing black uniforms with scarves around their necks. Why did you describe -- why do you say "Serbian soldiers"? If they were wearing black uniforms with scarves around their necks, they're paramilitaries, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement I said that in Bellanice village, paramilitaries, soldiers, and police forces entered my village, but I was beaten by the policemen. I was beaten three times within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, he may be. If you read the rest of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- particularly, the third-last complete line, is there not even more confusion about who is responsible for initiating this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's where I was trying to get, but I couldn't get through the first statement to get to the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's because the witness has the latter part in mind as well. So I think he has to be faced with the whole of this and then asked if he could clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First you tell us: "Two Serbian soldiers and paramilitaries in black uniforms and scarves around their necks, pulled you out of the car. You talk about have had a video camera and an audio recorder that were a gift. And then you say: "The police grabbed me by the throat and pulled me from the car." Now, did you --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, please, Your Honour. I did not give any gifts to anybody. Serbs do not deserve any gifts. Two policemen took those things forcibly from me. Don't laugh. Please, don't laugh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, you are misunderstanding the position. It's clearly said in your statement that you had received these items as gifts from another person. That's irrelevant. Just leave it out of consideration; it's quite clear in the statement. Concentrate on the two points where you have said who was responsible for removing you from the car. Now, you've said at one stage two Serbian soldiers and paramilitaries wearing black uniforms and scarves around their necks pulled me out of the car." You've then said: "Police grabbed me by the throat and pulled me out of the car." Now, we are confused about this and would like you to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the police entered our street, what I think I said was there were paramilitaries and soldiers, while I was pulled out of the car by two Serb policemen. I was taken into the basement; I was robbed. They took my camera and other equipment, journalistic equipment; money as well. And they also shot, fired, their guns in the basement. You can find the traces today there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's sufficient for the moment. Mr. Ackerman will undoubtedly have other questions to clarify the particular point, the particular point, that we are concerned about. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So are you saying now that it was the police that pulled you out of the car and not the Serb military/paramilitary that you talk about?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go on to another subject now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're also saying that the army and paramilitaries were there when this was happening, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your description of them is: "Two Serbian soldiers and paramilitaries came wearing black uniforms and scarves around their necks." That's what you've actually said. Now, that's a very confusing statement. What were they? Were they soldiers, these two people, or were they paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was pulled out from the car by the policemen. But around the area there, there were paramilitaries and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, regrettably, that's not clear from your statement but it's perhaps a little clearer now. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to your next statement in June of 2001. You talk about April 1st, again around 11.00, the village of Belanica and shelling of that village. You say that large military, paramilitary, and police Serb forces had burned and destroyed everything that was Albanian, property in the above-mentioned villages. And those villages must be something other than Belanica. Can you tell me what other villages you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the village Semetisht, Decan, Bllace, Banje, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you didn't actually see the burning and destruction of Albanian property in these villages at the time it was done, did you? You didn't see who was doing it?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that myself. That was done by the military and police forces, headed by the six accused here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh. They were there, were they? The six accused were there? You saw them there that day?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't present, but they were the ones who gave the orders for everything that happened in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, well tell us where you saw the orders. Where did you see those?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we're not going down this road. The answer given by the witness was it done by the military and police forces headed by the six accused here. All that amounts to is a statement that they had responsibilities for military and police forces. Let's concentrate on the issues that really concern us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, how on earth would he know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How would you know that? How would you know they had any responsibility for that? Did you see orders?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see them here amidst us; that's why they are here, to answer for their crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So just because they are sitting here, you've assumed they must be guilty. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had been -- had not been guilty, they wouldn't be in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure glad the Judges don't see this the way you do. So I guess you see your job here as -- to give evidence that would help confirm your belief that they are responsible in some way for what you say. Is that what you see your job here to be?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are responsible for the crimes committed in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that's your position. So when you say that you saw military, paramilitary, and police Serb forces, that's just a catch-all phrase that you use every time, because you know that that would help in your mission to assist in making these people behind me responsible for what happened. And that's why you use that. It's not because you saw all those forces, is it?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the Serb army and the police burning down entire, killing, massacring; killing even the livestock. I have got pictures in my possession to prove what the Serbs did in Kosova, charred houses. Is this not a crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 45 of your statement, the 2nd of April you were at the Morina border point, and you say: "A civilian Serb dressed in black, armed with a pistol, came up from the border point toward us." On what criteria do you conclude that this was a civilian Serb?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was a Serb. He didn't come there, but he was present and he was there for the purpose of ill-treating Albanians that they were kicking out of their own country. And he was the one who continually mistreated us. He wasn't an American, neither was he a German; he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you understand the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, your job here -- your job here is not as an advocate for any case; you're here as a witness. And I hope you will bear that very much in mind as you answer the questions. You were asked a specific question there, which was: "On what criteria do you conclude that this was a civilian Serb?" And you gave us no basis for reaching your conclusion. Now, if it was left at that, we would say: There's no evidence before us that that man was a Serb. Why don't you just listen to the questions and answer them? And I assure you, you will do far more good to the case the Prosecution are presenting than you will do by deciding that you will advocate a cause rather than answer questions. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you not understand the question to be: How did you determine this person was a civilian? Did you not understand the question?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing plain clothes, plain clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you said he was wearing -- he was dressed in black, and you've talked about paramilitary wearing black. What was the difference between his black clothes and paramilitary black clothes?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it would help if you waited until I finish my question before you start answering it, I think. Now, did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear the question. At this point in time, there's me here wearing black clothes, but he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For reasons which we don't need to determine at the moment, counsel want you to try to explain how you came to the conclusion that he was a Serb. Now, it may not sound a terribly sensible question to you, I don't know, but it is a question which is undoubtedly admissible in this Tribunal. Could you please try and assist us by answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Serb. I have no other comment to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In February of 2002, you did a very short witness statement where you made, what you called, a correction, with regard to an individual by the name of Zoran Lazic. In your -- in another statement you had said that Zoran Lazic was chairman of the municipality of Suhareke. And then you wanted to make a change to say what you meant to say was that Zoran Lazic was the chief criminal in the municipality of Suhareke. Can you explain that, why at one point you would call him the chairman of the municipality and then say, no, no, chief criminal?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said the "chief of municipality," I got that version from the KLA. But overnight, the Serbian police changed the personnel in the police, in the municipality, and everywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So some of the things the KLA told you that you have put in your statement turned out not to be true, right? Can I get an answer?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was it that transpired not to be true?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said that you got the original information about Zoran Lazic from the KLA; then you found out that wasn't the case, and that's why you changed it to "chief criminal." Or was it "chief criminal", the information you got from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that he was chairman, but overnight there were changes in Kosova. The heads of services -- of the internal services of Serbia were changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We're going to have to explore this just a little bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah. Well, we'll do it after we have a break, Mr. Ackerman. We lost some time at the last one, so we'll restrict this break and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00. Mr. Zogaj, we have to have a break at this stage for 20 minutes or so. Could you please accompany the usher; he will show you where to wait while we have this break. And we'll see you again at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, we were talking about that last correction statement that you gave regarding Zoran Lazic. And in answer to my question about that, you said this, and I have it on the screen here in front of me, so I want to be accurate. "When I said the 'chief of municipality,' I got that version from the KLA." That kind of makes it clear that you were having conversations with the KLA about what your testimony was going to be in this Tribunal. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I made the statement, I based it on information gathered from the KLA. I couldn't stay with other Albanians [as interpreted], and they knew that he was the chief of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction from the interpreter: I couldn't stay with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Part of the answer doesn't seem to make any sense where you say: When you made the statement, you based it on information gathered from the KLA. The transcript then says: "I couldn't stay with other Serbs, and they knew that he was the chief of that municipality." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Albanians. We Albanians could in no way mingle with the Serbs, solely with Albanians; and in the course of conversations we had with Albanians at the time, they told me that Lazic was chief of the municipality. I repeated it before and I shall repeat it again. Serbian policy changed its leaders overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find it difficult then to see how you jump from that to say he's the chief criminal. Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because he had been identified in the midst of the population as someone who'd committed crimes. Following the NATO bombardment on Kosova, on the 25th of March, in Suhareke and its surrounding villages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't go on on that subject. I -- if the matter -- if counsel wish to explore the matter further, they may do so. You're complete, Mr. Ackerman, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I am one of the attorneys for Mr. Lukic. I will have you some questions here today and I would kindly request you to pay close attention to my questions and give me the most concise and truthful answer possible so that we may move along as efficiently as possible. Now, first of all, you have just indicated that a portion of your statement was based on information that the KLA gave you. Are there other portion of this statement that are based upon the KLA; that is to say, are we to take this statement as being your recollection of what you saw and what you know or a report of what the KLA wanted the Court to hear?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only that bit of information that comes through my talks with the KLA; the rest of it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were here several weeks ago giving your direct examination, you identified at page 3792 of the transcript, line 23, you identified a particular tank as being a Serb police tank. And today I believe you also testified that you had brought pictures of the Serbian police uniforms and their tanks. Could you please help me out and describe for me what these Serbian police tanks looked like. How do you differentiate them from other tanks?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What colour would these Serbian police tanks be?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're not telling me, are you, that in the course of your time in Kosovo and Metohija, you actually saw blue police tanks operating anywhere in the municipalities where you were at?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 30.000 troops, police, army, and paramilitary, Serbs involved in Kosovo, and Sreten Lukic headed these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you about tanks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, have you with you a photograph of what you say was a Serb police tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you please let me see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a clarification, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give it to the usher, please. Give it to Mr. Ivetic first of all, please, so that he can see the actual exhibit, and then we shall put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this appears to be what is known as a BOV, rather than a tank. Is this the type of tank that you claim the Serbian police in Suva Reka utilised at the time you witnessed them in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what they were. I'm not a military man, and I cannot cite numbers and figures here. But yes, there was the type of vehicle that belonged to the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that this type of vehicle does not have armaments on it? There is no cannon on this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it had any, they'd show; if it doesn't have any cannons, it does have good enough --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the confusion I have relates to the vehicle that you described at transcript page 3792, line 23, because that vehicle was not this type of vehicle; that was an actual tank with a cannon on it. How do you explain that difference?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this picture in Pristina during protests organised in 1997; however, this type of weaponry and artillery belonging to the Serbian forces was operational throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is there some method of us preserving this that's on the ELMO and having it admitted as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is indeed, but before you move on you gave a quotation from page 3792. Did you mean to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what it shows on my version of it, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it not 3692?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mine says 3792. It's dealing with Exhibit P1325, if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness's evidence concluded on the copy I have at page 3699.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You know what, Your Honour, that may have been the day that we had that glitch with the transcript system, so that may be why we have different numbers. In any event, it's dealing with Exhibit P1325 which at that point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you're quoting our transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, our transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Milosevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting ours from the 22nd of September, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the photograph can be scanned from the ELMO and will be given an in-court exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC103, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you're finished with the photograph, it can be returned to the witness, since we have the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. I can move on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, just to be clear. We need to retain it until it's properly scanned, I'm sorry, and then it will be returned to you, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I assume I can proceed while that's being scanned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now I'd like to have Exhibit P1325 placed on e-court, the Exhibit that was discussed on the 22nd of September, 2006; and it will be page 2 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zogaj, on the 22nd of September, you were asked by the Prosecutor, at line 19, page 3792: "Can you say whether or not the vehicles you see here were vehicles that were used in the operation in Belanica?" "A. Yes. "Q. How many one of them? "A. The one here under number 5, it belonged to the Serbian police." Now, sir, the vehicle listed, in number 5, does not resemble in any way the vehicle you have just shown us a photograph of, does it?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph number 5, yes, it does belong to Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon what do you conclude that vehicle number 5 belongs to the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colour, from the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the colour, to me, appears to be green camouflage. Is it your testimony here today that the Serbian police drove around in tanks that were green camouflage? You earlier told us they were all blue.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This belonged to the police. This is a photograph of Serb -- of a Serbian police weapon. This is the type of weaponry used by the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have that evidence from you, Mr. Zogaj. The question being put to you is that you had earlier indicated that police vehicles were blue, and this one certainly is not blue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The camouflage, yes, it's blue and camouflage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps, I don't know if it would help if we zoom in a little bit more on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say that's blue camouflage, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are a number of colours here on this type of tank. There is blue, green; you can see something reddish or orange, white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you take any photographs of vehicles like this in the same way as you took the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have other photographs as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of this type of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We possess other photographs, which were left behind by Serbian forces after withdrawing from Kosova, and we do possess them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that. I'm talking about photographs that you personally took of vehicles as you observed them. Do you have any pictures you took of a vehicle like the one now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Luckily - and I said this at the beginning of the statement in Tirana - God-willing and should I be able to find the basement of my house intact, there we would be able to find facts of the crimes committed of the Serbs in Kosova. However, upon returning to Kosova, I found out that it had been burned out. There's a series of pictures here, which I can hand over, to demonstrate the traces left by the Serbs in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll take that as a no to the question I've asked. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't think that was a no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zogaj, if you refuse to answer my questions, I will simply treat them as a "no." My simple question is whether you have in your possession there a photograph you took of a which resembles the one on the screen. That's all I want to know at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not the same. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, I don't want to see it at the moment. That's a matter for counsel to raise with you if they wish. I have a particular question I wish answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a different type of weaponry. It's another type of an artillery weapon I'm holding aloft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which you say is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is similar in colour and, as I said before, I cannot distinguish the types of weaponry, not being of -- a military person myself. That's the type of weaponry used by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My concern is about police equipment at the moment. Now, are you saying that the photograph you have in your hand is of a weapon that was used by the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where was the photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We found this in Suhareke. We found it in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, I have made it abundantly clear. My question relates to photographs you personally took. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph I handed over earlier is one which I took myself, while the rest of the pictures that I took were, unfortunately, burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one more question with respect to this picture and then we can move on. Is it your testimony that this type of vehicle, even though you're not a military man, is the same type of vehicle as the other picture that you just showed us that you took in 1997? Is that your contention?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not the same. The picture showing on the screen is blue, and I think it belongs to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll just leave it at that and move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention now. In your statement of 1999, you describe how on the 20th of March, 1999, at 12.20 p.m., the first attacks began on the villages of Pecane, Studencane, and Doberdolan. Where were you located at this time, so as to be able to know what was going on in these three different villages at precisely the same time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the attack started, I was in Semetisht. And from Semetisht, I set out to go to Peqan, and I saw the Serb forces shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct then that all you saw was what happened -- strike that. Am I correct, then, that when you say in your statement on the 20th of March, 1999, at 12.20 p.m., the first attacks began, is your knowledge of that event limited to Pecane, your first-hand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say in the statement that it was only Peqan. I said also the surrounding village Studencane, Doberdolan, Semetisht, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about where you personally where and what you personally saw. You were in Pecane at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as far as what you personally saw on March 20th at 12.20 p.m., that's limited to Pecane. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw Peqan, but I saw the artillery firing towards those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you about Pecane, since you were in the area at that time. I'm sure that you must have seen or known of the fierce resistance to the Serb forces from the side of the local UCK/KLA during this time-period, specifically in Pecane. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA was at their own point, and it was protecting the civilian Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, sir, we have in evidence the statement of Mr. Ilmet Fondaj, the commander of the KLA in Pecane that states otherwise, that says that the KLA ordered the civilians in Pecane to leave so that they could ambush the Serbs in Pecane and in fact that they did do so. Does that refresh your recollection as to the situation in Pecane?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I doubt if that's a fair question. Your previous question was given, I think, a "yes" answer. Your question was "fierce resistance" from the KLA, and the answer was, yes, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can hardly criticise the witness now for answering that question the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I'm reading the same response, I had it translated to me that they were in the village protecting the Albanian civilian population, which we have evidence was not in Pecane, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you can't criticise the witness for making that point in answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. Perhaps, it's a poorly phrased question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, please, approach it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of an individual named Ilmet Fondaj?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that Ilmet Fondaj was a member of the KLA and the local KLA person in charge of Pecane village in the Suva Reka municipality in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have knowledge of the fact that Mr. Fondaj and his KLA contingent utilised a strategy, whereby they ordered their civilians to leave, so as to lay a trap or ambush for Serb forces in ethnic Albanian villages, including Pecane?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fondaj and the others did this because the military police and paramilitary Serb forces were shelling the village; and so that no civilians were hurt, they told the population to withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And isn't it a fact, sir, that from March 20th, 1999, the KLA forces in Pecane and the surrounding area fought with the Serb forces for a total of eight days in a row before finally withdrawing to Belanica and the mountain behind Belanica?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but the truth is a little bit different because the police, the army, and the paramilitaries started to shell these villages. They were the first. This is the truth, and the KLA was protecting the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The KLA was in the villages before the Serbs showed up, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that for this eight-day period, when the KLA was battling the Serb forces, am I correct that you were among the various villages in the municipality of Suva Reka and not in Suva Reka town itself?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 20th of March, nobody could enter Suhareke from quieter areas such as Nishor, Bellanice, Pagarusha, et cetera. It was not possible for us to enter Suhareke. We only observed from close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So am I correct then that you were not in Suva Reka on the 25th of March, 1999, which according to your statement from 1999 at page 3, paragraph 2, is when you claim to have seen certain events transpire in Suva Reka town?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw the civilian population leaving the town of Suhareke, because at that time, those moments, the population was in -- in Suhareke was being massacred, the houses were being set on fire, and I saw the civilian population leaving the town barefoot. It was in the early hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How far away from Suva Reka town were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any binoculars with you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any binoculars, but my mind was working, my body was working. I was observing everything from far, from the place I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And from 2 kilometres away, you didn't see anyone being massacred, did you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that, but as I said in my statement, I talked to the citizens that were living -- leaving Suhareke without even the bare minimal elements that are necessary for survival. This is what they told me, and this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So am I correct, then, that your entire description of what happened in Suhareke town after March 20th, 1999, that is all based upon what other people told you rather than anything you saw with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the fires, the burning, of Suhareke. This is a fact. And I believed the people who were coming in my direction and I talked to them and they spoke to me about their family members who had been killed. And, for example, Professor Sejdi Bytyqi, a professor of history, he was among the ones that were executed but he survived the massacre. All his friends were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have that in your statement, and now I'm satisfied with the fact that you did not eye-witness any of that. I'd like to move on now. Before we do, back to Pecane. You, in your statement, identify that - and this is the 1999 statement - relative to Pecane, you said as to the forces that entered: "These were not policemen wearing standard uniforms, but their uniforms seemed to be with different colours, more black than anything else. They were masked and they had painted faces." Did you, in fact, see these forces enter Pecane with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that. I know this, that the police forces were operating. The army forces and the paramilitary forces were also operating, and I saw them; this is the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading your statement, the top of page 3 in the English version, the 1999 statement, and the quotation I read is from there. Are you telling us now that you did not see policemen -- strike that. Are you telling me that you did not see individuals wearing uniforms of different colours, more black than anything else, that were masked and that had painted faces in Pecane; and are you not attributing those as being policemen?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They entered Peqan. What I think I said was that in Bellanice they had painted faces and bandannas. I don't think I said that about Peqan. I said that the forces entered Peqan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, if I can go back to page 2. It says: "I saw eight tanks in the village of Peqan alone; seven armoured vehicles and two Pragas, heavy gun mounted on top of an armoured vehicle. These were not policemen wearing standard uniforms, but their uniforms seemed to be with different colours, more black than anything else. They were masked and had painted faces. The people who directed these attacks included the following men ..." Now, sir, again I ask you: Is this an accurate description of the people you saw in Peqan?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I mentioned that regarding Pecane. I can tell you about Bellanice. I don't know about this figure; seven, or what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let me ask you a little more about Peqan. You identify an individual as Zika. Now, with respect to Zika, had you seen him wearing this type of uniform before; the type of uniform that's described here in your sworn statement from 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zika was a regular policeman. He was part of the Serbian police in Suhareke; and as far as I remember, I did not say this about Pecane. I said that this happened in Bellanice. And he took my car keys and they beat -- he beat me together with his friends. He was not wearing a mask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, so now he's the one that beat you; it's no longer the two soldiers and the paramilitaries in the black uniforms, or the two policemen. It's Zika that actually beat you in your car?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zika beat me the third time, because I said earlier that within half an hour I was beaten three times by the Serbian police. And at this moment, when Zika took my car keys, there were four policemen. He took my car and they used the car -- they roamed in the car all the time -- during all the time they stayed in Kosova. And I have a photograph of that car.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I'd like to ask you about Zika and these policemen that you have identified. Please describe their uniforms for me.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue uniforms of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I live in America, where the police in every city have a different colour uniform. I need for you to describe for me what it means when you say "blue uniforms of the police." Describe how those uniforms look, apart from the colour.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see any markings on these blue camouflage uniforms of these policemen that you said were there and either beat you or watched Zika beat you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They beat us mercilessly, and it was not possible for us to get any figures or -- and for me to be able to tell you today that this was the one or the other one did that. I only know that Zika was there. He had a blue camouflage uniform, and this is very true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I presume, sir, if they were beating you, they were rather close to you. Did you see anything on their uniforms from which you could conclude that they were police?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were policemen; they were. It is easy to tell a policeman from a soldier, a soldier from a paramilitary, and so on and so forth. And I think that's that. He was a Serb policeman wearing a blue camouflage uniform. He was not wearing a mask; unmasked, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What, if anything, did these policemen you've identified on their uniforms have on their chest?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the protection; what you call -- how do you call them? You call them flak jackets, I suppose. They were armed; they had a Kalashnikov automatic rifle, pistols. They had knives and pliers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this description applying to Zika and the two other individuals who pulled you out of your car and beat you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It applies to the rest as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What colour was this flak jacket or vest?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did these uniforms that these individuals were wearing, did they have anything on their shoulders or their sleeves; and if so, please tell me?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cyrillic script, in Serbian language, if I'm not mistaken, there was something that, if I'm not wrong, was criminal, criminal police or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did they have any other emblems? And I did not ask you to look at any pictures, so I don't know what you're looking at that, sir. But I would ask you, based upon your recollection, did they have any other emblems anywhere on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the Serbian emblem, the emblem of the police, the army, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They had all these emblems on their uniform?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paramilitaries didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about the individuals that you have identified as police in these blue camouflage uniforms. What type of emblems did you see on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flag of Serbia or Yugoslavia or whatever it was. That was the one. That's how we were able to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, I am going to have to interrupt you as long as this is a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because we have one matter, as you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to deal with separately from this. Mr. Zogaj, we have to bring your evidence to a close for the day at this stage because another case will be taking place this afternoon which occupies one of our Judges. So you will have to return on Monday to continue your evidence. I think that is in the morning on Monday. Is that correct? Monday morning at 9.00. So you need to be back in this building in good time to resume giving evidence at 9.00 on Monday morning. Meanwhile, it's vital that you have no discussion with anyone at all about your evidence, that is either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give in the case. You can talk about whatever you like to whomever you like, but you must not discuss with anyone any part of the evidence. Now, could you please leave the court with the usher, and we'll see you again at 9.00 on Monday morning. The court will now go into private session to deal with the application in relation to the witness.
